evidence: Traupman 29: cadere in probātiōne, to flunk a test
Traupman 30: probātiōnem sustinēre, to pass a test
terms.comment: Classically a trial or inspection, of athletes or recruits; Traupman’s word for a test. To pass a test is probātiōnem sustinēre, to fail it in probātiōne cadere (Traupman 29, 30; see fail); to study for one, ad probātiōnem sē parāre (Morgan–Owens).

evidence: M-O s.v. test: exam, examination, after Grosse (1846) and Egger
terms.comment: Classically a swarm of bees, then the tongue of a balance, and so a weighing (Pers. 1.6; Ov. Met. 9.552, Lewis & Short). To take an exam is exāmen subīre, to pass it exāmen superāre (Morgan–Owens).

evidence: Ter. Eun. 476: fac perīclum in litterīs
terms.comment: With facere, to put to the test; its everyday sense is danger.

evidence: Levi–Bini p. 271: experīmentum Latīnī sermōnis, an exam in Latin
terms.comment: A proof or trial, mostly after Augustus (Quint. 2.5.15, Lewis & Short); Levi and Bini’s word for a school exam.
Classically “to weigh”, of scales and of thought (Cic. Tusc. 1.43, Lewis & Short); of testing pupils it is modern.

evidence: Cic. de Or. 1.102: quaestiunculam alicui pōnere (Lewis & Short)

phrases.latin: Fac perīclum in litterīs, fac in palaestrā, in mūsicīs.
phrases.english: Test him in letters, test him at wrestling, in music.
